title: Build Logic with Pseudocode and Decomposition
learningObjectives: Translate a problem statement into language-neutral pseudocode steps
Decompose a large algorithm into focused reusable methods
Define method inputs, outputs and observable behavior clearly
Trace sample data through each algorithm step systematically
State invariants that should remain true during processing

understand.concept: Pseudocode describes an algorithm without Java syntax. Decompose a task into named steps and methods with clear inputs and outputs. Trace a small example and check that each step preserves the intended invariant.
understand.whyItMatters: Build Logic with Pseudocode and Decomposition helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain. It connects core language knowledge with realistic programming tasks.
understand.analogy: Treat this concept as a clearly labeled tool: select it for a specific responsibility and check the result.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy is only a learning aid; actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Pseudocode separates the idea from Java syntax

Pseudocode describes algorithm steps in plain, structured language. It is not compiled and does not require Java punctuation or exact API names. Its purpose is to make decisions, repetition, inputs and outputs understandable before implementation. Use consistent words such as READ, IF, REPEAT, RETURN and DISPLAY.

## Decompose work into focused operations

Break a larger problem into smaller responsibilities. Each method should have a clear purpose, explicit parameters and a meaningful return value or documented side effect. For a student report, separate reading input, validating scores, calculating an average and formatting the report. This makes each operation easier to reason about and test independently.

## Trace data and preserve invariants

Choose a small input and trace the algorithm one step at a time in a table. Record important variables before and after each step. An invariant is a condition that should remain true throughout a loop or operation. In a second-largest-distinct-number algorithm, the stored largest value should remain at least as large as the stored second-largest value after every processed element.

## Translate and verify

Translate each pseudocode operation into Java statements and methods. Keep the same sequence and conditions, then compare the Java program with the hand trace. Test duplicates, empty or very small inputs, and boundary values. If the trace is confusing, simplify the algorithm before adding more code.

examples.title: Core concept
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int subtotal = 200; int tax = subtotal / 10; System.out.println(subtotal + tax); } }
examples.explanation: Calculates a subtotal, tax amount and final total.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int[] values = {2, 4, 6}; int sum = 0; for (int value : values) sum += value; System.out.println(sum); } }
examples.explanation: Decomposes aggregation into initialization, traversal and accumulation.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { java.util.function.IntUnaryOperator doubleValue = value -> value * 2; System.out.println(doubleValue.applyAsInt(7)); } }
examples.explanation: Extracts a focused operation into a reusable functional value.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int balance = 100; int withdrawal = 30; if (withdrawal <= balance) balance -= withdrawal; System.out.println(balance); } }
examples.explanation: Preserves an invariant: a withdrawal cannot exceed the available balance.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String[] steps = {"read", "validate", "calculate", "display"}; for (int i=0; i<steps.length; i++) System.out.println((i+1)+". "+steps[i]); } }
examples.explanation: Represents an algorithm as ordered steps before implementing each step.

practise.guidedTask: Write pseudocode for finding the second-largest distinct number. Trace it using a normal list, duplicates and a one-element list, then translate it into Java methods.
practise.independentTask: Decompose a student-report problem into input parsing, validation, calculation and formatting methods. Define each method's inputs and output.
hints: Write language-neutral steps using clear READ, IF, REPEAT and RETURN operations.
Split the algorithm into methods with one responsibility and explicit parameters and results.
Trace a small example and state an invariant that should remain true during repetition.
practise.challenge: Extend the algorithm with an invariant that explains why the current largest and second-largest values remain correct after each iteration.

options: A language-neutral description of algorithm steps
questions.answer: A language-neutral description of algorithm steps
questions.explanation: Pseudocode expresses the algorithm independently of Java syntax, allowing the logic to be reviewed before implementation.

questions.prompt: Why decompose a large problem into methods?
options: Each method can have a focused responsibility and be tested separately
It guarantees fewer lines in every program
It removes the need for names
questions.answer: Each method can have a focused responsibility and be tested separately
questions.explanation: Decomposition gives each method a focused responsibility, making the behavior easier to understand, reuse and test separately.

questions.prompt: What should a method contract describe?
options: Its inputs, output and relevant behavior
questions.answer: Its inputs, output and relevant behavior
questions.explanation: A useful method contract states its inputs, result and relevant behavior or side effects so callers know what to expect.

questions.prompt: What does tracing an example by hand help verify?
options: The sequence of state changes and algorithm logic
questions.answer: The sequence of state changes and algorithm logic
questions.explanation: A hand trace records each state change and reveals whether the algorithm follows the intended sequence for a known input.

options: A condition that should remain true at a defined point or throughout an algorithm
A variable that must always be public
A comment that cannot be edited
questions.answer: A condition that should remain true at a defined point or throughout an algorithm
questions.explanation: An invariant is a condition that must remain true at a specified point or throughout each iteration of an algorithm.
